opus-5.5.text:
I think for me, taste isn't only about which problem you choose or which idea you believe in. It's also about how you present it, because the way you communicate a piece of work is part of the work itself.

When I write a paper, I spend a lot of time on the figures, the layout, even the colors and fonts. Some people think that's superficial, like decoration on top of the real research. But I see it differently. If you can't make a clean, beautiful figure that explains your idea, that often means you don't fully understand the idea yet. The process of designing the presentation forces you to distill what really matters. What's the one message? What can I remove? That's the same kind of judgment you need when doing the research.

There's also a respect element. A paper is something you're asking other people to spend their time reading. Thousands of researchers might look at it. So I feel a responsibility to make it as clear and pleasant to read as possible. If the work is good but the presentation is messy, a lot of people will just miss the point.

And honestly, I think good research has an aesthetic quality. The best ideas in our field, things like ResNet, are simple and elegant. When the idea is elegant, the presentation should reflect that elegance too. So style and substance aren't separate for me. Caring about how something looks and reads is a signal that you care about getting it right, and I think that attitude carries over into everything: how you design experiments, how you write code, how you think about problems. That's why I consider it part of taste.

r001.rationale: The candidate says paper presentation—including figures, layout, colors, and fonts—is part of research taste and reflects the same judgment as the research itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think a lot of people see the design of a paper — the figures, the layout, how the first page looks — as decoration, something you do at the end if there's time. I've never seen it that way. To me, how you present a piece of work is inseparable from how you think about it.

When I'm making a figure, I'm forced to ask: what is the one thing I want someone to take away from this? If I can't draw it cleanly, usually that means I don't actually understand the idea cleanly yet. So the design process becomes a kind of debugging for the research itself. Many times I've gone back and changed experiments, or even reframed the whole paper, because I couldn't make the figure honest and simple at the same time.

There's also a question of respect for the reader. Researchers are flooded with papers now. If someone gives you ten minutes of their attention, you owe them clarity. A good first-page figure, a clean table, a consistent visual language — these lower the cost of understanding. I think that's part of doing science well, not separate from it. The goal is not to impress, it's to communicate, and communicating well requires taste: knowing what to leave out, what to emphasize, where to stop.

And honestly, taste in research is about choosing problems and choosing what matters. Design is the same muscle. Deciding that a result deserves a full figure versus a footnote, deciding that a method is simple enough to explain in one diagram — those are judgment calls about what's important. So when students in my group spend a lot of time on how a paper looks, I don't treat it as wasted effort. I treat it as them learning to think about what they actually believe is the core contribution. Over time, that habit shapes what kind of work they choose to do in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly connects paper design to research taste, saying design uses the same judgment about what matters and that choices about emphasis express what researchers believe is the core contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste shows up in what you choose to emphasize and what you choose to leave out. That applies to the research question, but it also applies to how you present the work. What is the central idea? What figure would make that idea clear? Which details are essential for understanding it?

For me, working on the design of a paper is a way of asking those questions again. If I can’t make a clear figure or explain the motivation simply, sometimes that means I haven’t understood the idea deeply enough myself. The process of presenting it can actually help sharpen the research.

And you’re asking people to spend their time reading your work. I think it’s worth putting care into that experience. A beautiful layout can’t rescue a weak idea, of course. But when the presentation is clear and thoughtful, it helps people see what matters. That connection between the idea and how you communicate it is why I consider design part of research taste.

r001.rationale: The candidate says paper design is part of research taste and explains that choices about presentation express what the researcher emphasizes and how they communicate the central idea.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste shows up in the choices you make: what problem you work on, what you think is important, and how you communicate it. The style of a paper is part of that communication. What do you put in the first figure? What can you leave out? What is the one idea you want someone to remember?

Making those decisions forces you to understand your own work more clearly. Sometimes you try to draw a simple figure and realize that your explanation is actually quite complicated, or that you haven’t identified the central point yet. So the design process can help sharpen the research itself.

And you’re asking people to spend their time understanding your work. A clear figure, a readable layout, a carefully written explanation—those are ways of respecting that time. Making something look nice doesn’t make the research good, but presenting a good idea well is part of doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response says research taste shows up in choices about how to communicate research, and identifies paper style and design as part of that communication.
